tagline.text: A grassy ridge trail crossing peaks strung together like a dinosaur's spine

location.label: Location
location.text: Nasugbu, Batangas (southwest of Tagaytay, near the Cavite border)

children.text: At about

above sea level, Mount Batulao is Batangas' signature day hike, its twelve jagged peaks strung together along a grassy ridge. Close to Tagaytay and popular for a traverse linking two trails, it draws everyone from beginners to seasoned hikers.
Mount Batulao rises to about

in Nasugbu, Batangas province, sitting along the route down from the Tagaytay highlands to the Nasugbu coast. Formed by volcanic activity long ago and worn down over the ages, it now stands as a row of sharp rock peaks, its jagged silhouette resembling a dinosaur's spine when seen from a distance. One story traces the name to the Tagalog words "bato" (rock) and "ilaw" (light).

Most of the mountain is a grassy ridge covered in tall grass, so the view stays open the whole way. From the ridge, you can look one way toward the Tagaytay highlands and Taal Lake, and the other toward the Nasugbu plains and Balayan Bay, with Mount Pico de Loro visible on a clear day. The grass turns golden in the dry season and deep green after the rains, so the same mountain shows a different face each season.

There are two trails: the "New Trail," which crosses a series of gentle peaks, and the "Old Trail," which has a steep section near the summit where you climb up and down holding onto ropes. The most popular route is a traverse — up the New Trail to the summit, then down the Old Trail — covering about
12km
in
5–7 hours
. All hikers are now required to climb with a local guide.

Reachable from Manila with a single bus ride, it suits people preparing for their first hike, expats wanting a light weekend workout, and travelers who love ridge-line photography. That said, it's a more demanding hike than it looks, given the exposed ridge with almost no shade and the midday heat and sun.
Climbing the gentle New Trail and descending the Old Trail, with its rope section, lets you experience both faces of the mountain. It's far more varied than an out-and-back on the same trail.

blocks.title: A ridge trail over the peaks

children.text: There's a particular pleasure in climbing over one small peak after another, passing numbered camps along the way. Looking back, the ridge you've crossed stretches out behind you like a wave.
Resting at a summit stall over a halo-halo or buko (coconut) juice is one of this mountain's small pleasures. The plains of Batangas and Cavite spread out in every direction.
Near the summit on the Old Trail side, a rocky slope of 60–70 degrees requires climbing up and down while holding a rope. It's short but thrilling, the highlight of the mountain.
Setting out around
5 AM
, when the registration station opens, lets you watch the sunrise from the ridge and reach the summit before the heat sets in.

Pitching a tent for the night at a designated campsite lets you see the lights of Tagaytay and Nasugbu after dark, and a sea of clouds in the morning. Check camping rules and fees at the registration station.
On a hill right below the mountain, Caleruega Church is a well-known small chapel set against the backdrop of Mount Batulao. It's a good place to rest quietly after your descent.
Take a bus from Buendia or PITX in Manila bound for Nasugbu
Get off at the KC Hillcrest (formerly Evercrest) entrance, take a tricycle to the jump-off
Register and get assigned a guide, start up the New Trail
Cross the ridge peaks, rest at a camp point, take in the view after sunrise
Reach the summit, halo-halo, buko juice, and snacks at a stall
Descend via the Old Trail, pass through the rope section
Finish the descent, shower and change
Head to Tagaytay for bulalo, or stop by Caleruega Church
Depart by bus or car for Manila
Hiking time varies widely, from
4–8 hours
, depending on fitness and crowds. Beginners can also simply go up and back down the New Trail, which is plenty. On weekends, expect to queue at the rope section, so plan with extra time.
Take a bus (DLTB and others) bound for Nasugbu from the terminal near LRT's Gil Puyat (Buendia) station in Pasay, or from PITX. Departures run frequently from early morning, taking about
2 hours 30 minutes–3 hours 30 minutes
, for a one-way fare of about
As the bus passes Tagaytay and heads down toward Nasugbu, tell the driver in advance to let you off at the entrance to "KC Hillcrest" golf course, formerly known as "Evercrest."
From the golf course entrance to the jump-off (registration station) is about
10–15 minutes
by tricycle, for about

per person. Since descending via the Old Trail brings you out at a different point, it helps to arrange your return tricycle at the registration station in advance. After the descent, catch another bus to Nasugbu or Manila from the roadside.
From Manila, take CAVITEX or SLEX up to Tagaytay, then follow the Tagaytay–Nasugbu road down. It's about
, taking about
2–2.5 hours
at pre-dawn hours, and private parking near the jump-off runs about
. Hiking groups often charter a 12-seater van for the day, for about
The best time is the dry season,
November–April
December–February
in particular is pleasant for ridge hiking, with cool morning temperatures around
and a breeze. During
March–May
, the grass turns brown and the sun is very strong, so the exposed ridge takes a real toll at midday. This is a good period to start at dawn and finish the descent by late morning.
In the
June–October

rainy season, the dirt trails turn to mud, making the steep sections and rope climb on the Old Trail especially slippery. On the plus side, the grassland turns a deep, vivid green for photos. If you hike during the rainy season, choose an out-and-back on the New Trail, and come down early since afternoon thunderstorms are frequent. Typhoon or heavy-rain warnings will close the trail.

On weekends and holidays, especially dry-season weekends, crowds bottleneck at the rope section and along the narrow ridge. Choose a weekday for a quieter hike. Operating policy may differ during Holy Week and the year-end holidays, so check the latest notices.

Most hikers go and return the same day, but if a pre-dawn bus doesn't appeal, staying in Tagaytay the night before is the easiest option. The area around Tagaytay's ridge road has everything from budget guesthouses to hotels, at about
per night, about
30–40 minutes
by car from the jump-off. If you want to spend a night on the mountain, you can pitch a tent at a designated campsite; a rented tent costs about
per night.

Along the trail and near the summit, small stalls run by locals sell water, soft drinks, halo-halo, buko, and simple snacks. Stalls sometimes close for the day, though, so be sure to bring your own water and trail food. After the descent, the classic move is to head up to Tagaytay for hot bulalo beef bone soup, Tagaytay's famous buko pie, and tawilis, a freshwater fish from Taal Lake. If you head down toward Nasugbu instead, grilled fish and seafood at a coastal restaurant are also good.
A guide is mandatory. Guides can be in short supply on weekends, so book ahead through the registration station or a local guide's contact.
Bring at least
2L
of water per person. Stalls exist, but prices are high, and water runs out fast in the midday dry-season heat.
There's almost no shade on the ridge, so bring a wide-brimmed hat, sunscreen, arm sleeves, and sunglasses.
Gloves help a lot on the Old Trail's rope section — they keep your palms from getting scraped and let you grip the rope firmly.
Wear trekking shoes with good grip. The dusty dry-season descent can be as slippery as sand. Trekking poles also help protect your knees.
Registration fees, guide fees, and stalls all take cash only, so bring plenty of small bills.
Packing a change of clothes and a towel for after the descent makes for a much more comfortable bus ride home.
Carry out all your trash, including bottles and wrappers from anything you buy at the stalls.
The rope section on the Old Trail is very steep. Cross one person at a time under your guide's direction, and turn back toward the New Trail if it's rained recently or your energy is running low.
The ridge is fully exposed to the sun, carrying a high risk of heat stroke. If you feel dizzy or get a headache, rest immediately and replenish fluids and electrolytes.
The open ridge is vulnerable to lightning strikes during afternoon thunderstorms. If you hear thunder, come down off the peak, stay low, and follow your guide's judgment.
The dry-season grassland catches fire easily. Never smoke or light a fire on the mountain.
The sides of the ridge drop off steeply, so don't step off the trail's edge for a photo. Be especially careful on windy days.
Registration fees, guide rules, and operating status change from time to time. Check the latest notices through the Nasugbu tourism office or a local guide before you go.
